criteria.statement: Strict walk: a strict project refuses merges without acceptance/review receipts (the flagless refusal cites quality_profile=strict) and passes with full evidence.
Legacy exception stays honest: absent receipts print labelled UNMEASURED lines (never a quality PASS), and stale or corrupt receipts refuse under both profiles.
Profile lifecycle: greenfield defaults strict, brownfield stays legacy, and an explicit owner choice survives re-init.
Wiring present in the merged sources: strict refusal attribution in merge gating and precise QUALITY refusal classes in clean classification.

findings.summary: Acceptance splits the five-test suite into three bounded node --test name-pattern criteria: the tool caps each criterion command at 60s and the run at 120s, so the full suite cannot run as one criterion; coverage still spans all five tests plus a wiring check.

clean classification matches precise QUALITY refusal classes, so the new UNMEASURED/VERIFIED accounting lines cannot be misread as failures; the conflict and quarantine suites keep their historic labels.

A missing or unreadable config degrades merge gating to legacy by design (same posture as the quarantine registry: the oracle must not change behavior on state it cannot read); the absence path is exercised by the legacy exception tests.

Machinery-focused suites and the pilot/dogfood fixtures opt into legacy explicitly (one commented line each, deliberate scope choice); the strict default is witnessed by the new suite and by self-cycle's full evidence walk. The test fallout is inherent to flipping an init default.

Battery on this slice's sources: npm test 327/327 at the implementation tip; audit 154 checks / 0 findings; pilot 44/44; dogfood 72 steps / 0 unexpected; self-cycle 61/61 including the strict walk (the runner script added afterwards is exercised by GREEN and the acceptance criteria). RED was re-recorded against the self-building runner because the merge oracle replays proofs in a dist-less merged tree; both tdd-red events remain in state history.
